feedback.problem:
Aluminum-26 has a half-life of $0.717$ million years. A sample of aluminum-26 has an initial mass of $40\,\mu \text{g}.$ Rounded to **one decimal place**, what is the mass of the sample after $1$ million years?

The mass of the sample after $1$ million years is approximately
{{field-1}}
$\mu \text{g}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=0.717$ million years, we have

$$
0.717=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{0.717}.
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=40\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=40{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/0.717}.
$$

Finally,

$$
M(1)=40{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2/0.717}≈15.2,
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Therefore, we conclude that the mass of the sample remaining after $1$ million years is approximately $15.2\,\mu \text{g}.$
